extracted.intended_audience: researchers (medical/health sciences), students, and clinicians planning or writing narrative/literature reviews
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, deciding when to use, and writing narrative (topic/literature) reviews in medical/health research, emphasizing differences from systematic/scoping reviews and pointing to resources for quality assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a narrative review
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative reviews (sometimes called a topic or literature review) are general discussions of a topic, often with no stated hypothesis. They are often invited papers written by experts in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative reviews can provide rationales for future research and can speculate on new types of interventions available. Citation: Rossella Ferrari (2015) Writing narrative style literature reviews, Medical Writing, 24:4, 230-235.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative reviews are a distinct study type (not 'less good' systematic reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative review is not a 'less good' systematic/scoping review. The aims and methodology are different; they are different study types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat narrative reviews as inferior — choose study type based on aims and methodology rather than perceived hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations — lack of methodology reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative reviews often do not include methodology (i.e., how did they get these results?), which can make them subjective in study selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because methodology is often absent, narrative reviews can be subjective and may not make their search and selection processes transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations — susceptibility to selection bias and subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective study selection can potentially lead to bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subjectivity makes narrative reviews not reproducible and may make it difficult to discern how much weight to apply to their claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose a narrative review — question too broad
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a narrative review when the research question is too broad for a comprehensive, methodologically rigorous systematic review to take place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative reviews suit broad topics where SR methodology would be infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose a narrative review — insufficient literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a narrative review when there is not enough literature yet available to perform a systematic review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative review to summarize and interpret limited or emerging bodies of literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose a narrative review — limited time or resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a narrative review when there is not enough time to perform a systematic review or when there is not a large enough team available to perform a SR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical constraints (time, team size) can justify a narrative approach, but be explicit about limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and authority considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative reviews are often invited papers written by experts in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert authorship can lend insight and authoritative synthesis, but may also introduce author perspective bias; declare expertise and potential conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality variability and available assessment resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Because there are no formal guidelines that narrative reviews must adhere to (such as PRISMA for systematic reviews) their quality can vary greatly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult resources to improve/report quality: 'Writing narrative style literature reviews' (Ferrari, 2015) and SANRA — a scale for the quality assessment of narrative review articles.
